definition: A stack of layers, each multiplying its input by a matrix of learned numbers (parameters) and applying a simple non-linear function. The matrix multiplications are what GPUs accelerate.
The neural-network design behind modern language models: a stack of identical layers, each with an attention block (tokens look at earlier tokens) and a feed-forward block where most parameters live.
The part of a transformer layer where each token compares itself with earlier tokens to pick up context. Its cost and its memory (the KV cache) grow with sequence length.
One learned number inside a model. 'A 405B model' has 405 billion of them; training adjusts them and inference reads them for every token generated.
Running inputs through every layer of the model to produce a prediction. Costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token.

Walking the layers in reverse to compute how each parameter should change to reduce the error (the gradient). Costs about twice the forward pass, so training totals about 6 FLOPs per parameter per token.
The single number that measures how wrong the model's predictions were on a batch; training tries to push it down.
For each parameter, the direction and size of the change that would reduce the loss. Gradients from all GPUs are averaged every training step.
The algorithm that turns gradients into parameter updates. It often keeps extra running statistics per parameter, which costs memory.
The standard optimizer for large models. It keeps two running averages per parameter (momentum and variance), which is why training needs about 16 bytes per parameter in mixed precision.

An intermediate result produced by a layer during the forward pass and kept for the backward pass. Activation memory grows with batch size and sequence length; recomputation trades it for extra compute.
Doing the heavy arithmetic in a compact number format (BF16 or FP8) while keeping a full-precision (FP32) master copy of the weights so small updates are not lost.
A 16-bit (2-byte) number format with the same range as 32-bit floats but less precision; the default format for training and much inference on current GPUs.
An 8-bit (1-byte) floating-point format supported by tensor cores since Hopper. It halves memory and roughly doubles tensor throughput versus BF16, with care needed to preserve accuracy.
The share of a GPU's theoretical peak FLOPS that turns into useful model arithmetic during training. Large training runs typically achieve about 35-45%.
A collective operation in which every GPU contributes a set of numbers (e.g. gradients) and every GPU receives the combined result. Its speed depends on the network between GPUs.
NVIDIA Collective Communications Library: the software that runs all-reduce, all-gather and similar operations across GPUs over NVLink, InfiniBand or Ethernet.
A snapshot of a model's weights and optimizer state saved to storage so a training job can restart after a failure without starting over.
The useful output of a system after losses: in training, the share of GPU-hours that actually advance the model; in serving, the throughput that still meets latency targets.
Empirical findings that model quality improves predictably (as a power law) with more parameters, data and compute. They justify ever-larger training budgets.
The 2022 finding that, for a fixed compute budget, parameters and training tokens should grow together, at roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
Deliberately training a model on far more tokens than the Chinchilla-optimal ratio so a smaller model reaches high quality and is cheaper to serve.
Everything done to a model after pre-training on raw text: instruction tuning, preference tuning and reinforcement learning. A growing share of total training compute.

Training by trial and reward: the model generates many candidate answers, they are scored (e.g. by checking a math result or running code), and the model is updated toward the better ones. RL runs contain large inference workloads.

A model design that routes each token to a few of many expert sub-networks, so only a fraction of parameters is active per token (DeepSeek-V3: 37B of 671B). Saves compute but still needs memory for all experts and fast all-to-all networking.
